extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of theology and biblical interpretation; clergy and learned readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close, scholarly exposition of the signification of the biblical terms 'body', 'spirit', 'angel', 'inspiration', and 'kingdom of God', giving rules for when each term should be understood literally, metaphorically, corporally, or as a vision/dream. Aimed at guiding correct exegesis of scriptural passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine constant signification of words in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing the foundation of all true Ratiocination, is the constant Signification of words; which in the Doctrine following, dependeth not (as in naturall science) on the Will of the Writer, nor (as in common conversation) on vulgar use, but on the sense they carry in the Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proceeding, determine from the Bible the meanings of ambiguous words (e.g., BODY, SPIRIT). Exegesis should rely on scriptural sense rather than author's private will or vulgar usage; ambiguities must be resolved from Scripture contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body (proper/scriptural sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Word Body, in the most generall acceptation, signifieth that which filleth, or occupyeth some certain room, or imagined place; and dependeth not on the imagination, but is a reall part of that we call the Universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodies are subjects to change (accidents) and are corporeal/substantial; 'substance incorporeall' is a contradiction. When interpreting biblical passages, 'body' should be taken as that which has dimension, place, and can be divided into parts, unless the scriptural sense clearly requires otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit (common and metaphoric senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: In common speech, Spirit may mean either a subtile, fluid, and invisible Body, or a Ghost, or other Idol or Phantasme of the Imagination; metaphorically it can mean disposition of mind, eminent ability, passion, or disease of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of metaphorical senses: disposition/inclination (e.g., 'a spirit of contradiction'), inclination to godliness ('the Spirit of God'), eminent ability ('the Spirit of Wisdome'), madness ('possessed with a spirit'). If none of these fit, the place may be beyond human understanding and is to be accepted by faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit of God as wind or breath (literal/phenomenal reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spirit of God may be taken for a Wind, (that is an Aire or Spirit Moved,) e.g., Gen. 1.2 'The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the Waters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where motion or diminution of waters is described, understand 'spirit' as an acting wind or external phenomenon rather than God himself moving (which would ascribe place to God). Compare similar passages (Gen. 8.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as extraordinary gifts of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spirit of God is sometimes used for extraordinary understanding or gifts of wisdom and skill (e.g., Joseph in Gen. 41.38; craftsmen filled with the Spirit of Wisdom in Exod. 28.3; Isaiah 11.2,3 lists 'Spirit of wisdom and understanding').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret passages describing 'Spirit' granting wisdom or craft as referring to giftedness or divine endowment of abilities, not necessarily to an incorporeal indwelling substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as extraordinary affections (zeal, courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some passages the Spirit of God denotes extraordinary zeal or courage in defense of God's people (e.g., Judges' heroes, Saul's fury in 1 Sam.11.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scripture attributes sudden fervor, fury, or zeal to the 'Spirit of God', read it as extraordinary affective states produced by God's action rather than literal possession by a ghostly entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as gift of prediction by dreams and visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where prophets speak by 'the Spirit of God' the knowledge of the future was often communicated by some supernatural Dream or Vision, not by a ghost speaking within them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret prophetic 'inspiration' as supernaturally granted dreams/visions that convey knowledge, distinguishing these from literal internal spirits speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as life (breath of life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spirit sometimes signifies life itself or the breath of life (e.g., Gen. 2.7 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read phrases like 'as long as the Spirit of God is in my nostrils' as idioms for being alive; 'spirit' here = vital breath or life-force, not an incorporeal ghost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as subordination to authority (institutional/representative sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: At times 'spirit' denotes a delegated authority or submission to a superior's appointment (e.g., the Spirit being put upon the seventy elders, Joshua full of the Spirit because Moses laid hands on him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'spirit' is associated with ordination, succession, or carrying on delegated duties, interpret it as authority or lawful commission rather than an ontological infusion of divine substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit as aerial/corporeal subtile bodies (apparitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciples who saw Jesus walking on the sea supposed him to be a 'Spirit' meaning an aerial body (a subtle corporeal apparition), not a mere phantasm, since many saw him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounts are common to many observers (not private fancies), consider reading 'spirit' as a subtil corporeal apparition formed by God, i.e., a thin body with dimensions, rather than a mere imaginary ghost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angel defined as Messenger (sign of God's extraordinary presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the name of ANGEL, is signified generally, a Messenger; most often a Messenger of God: any thing that makes known his extraordinary Presence, especially by a Dream, or Vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations of 'angel' include: a voice or cloud as 'angel' when it signifies God's presence; apparitions in dreams/visions called angels; some scriptural 'angels' are actually God himself speaking. Do not assume created, permanent, incorporeal beings from every mention of angels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angels: permanence and materiality judged from Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no canonical Old Testament text (held by the Church of England) proving angels are permanent, immaterial beings without quantity; many passages support angels being substantial and capable of being in places and punished (e.g., 1 Cor.6.3; 2 Pet.2.4; Jude 1.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read references to angels in light of texts that imply permanence and materiality (e.g., judgment, chains, punishment); avoid construing 'angel' uniformly as immaterial nothingness. Consider context: some 'angels' are visions, some may be created corporeal ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration (proper vs metaphorical usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: INSPIRATION properly would mean blowing in of a thin aire; scriptural use is metaphorical: God 'inclined' the minds of writers to write useful things for teaching, reproving, correcting. Prophecy by the Holy Spirit is best understood as voice in a Dream or Vision, not as infusion of God's substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take 'inspiration' as literal transfer of divine substance into writers; treat it as God disposing minds or granting prophetic dreams/visions. Avoid the improper literal sense 'infused' as if graces were bodies to be carried around.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God: prefer proper (political/covenantal) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdome of God in Scripture most often signifies a Kingdom properly so named — a polity constituted by the votes/covenant of God's people (e.g., the covenant with Abraham, renewal at Sinai), rather than merely eternal felicity or metaphoric sanctification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting 'kingdom of God', give weight to historical/covenantal texts that indicate earthly, civil sovereignty by pact (God as King over a peculiar people). Recognize later metaphorical uses (dominion over sin, kingdom of grace) primarily in New Testament contexts but prefer the proper political sense where the scriptural context supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and nature of God's kingdom as covenantal commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of the kingdom of God is the covenant with Abraham (Gen.17), renewed by Moses at Sinai (Exod.19.5) making Israel 'a Peculiar people' and a 'Sacerdotall Kingdome' — a commonwealth instituted by pact, setting them apart for God's special service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret references to God's kingdom in light of covenant theology: it denotes a people set apart by oath/consent, with distinct civil and religious structures (e.g., high priest as viceroy). Scriptural examples (Samuel, Isaiah, Micah, Ezekiel, Luke) support an earthly dimension to this kingship.
